newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's Lebed may learn from Ivan the Terrible.
newsitem.headline: Russia's Lebed may learn from Ivan the Terrible.

text.p: Potential Russian strongman Alexander Lebed, enjoying some free time after being dumped by President Boris Yeltsin, went to the theatre on Friday and may have learned a lesson from one of the country's most notorious rulers.

The charismatic former security chief and would-be president entered Moscow's elegant Maly Theatre to loud applause from other theatre-goers before the curtain rose on A.K.Tolstoy's "Death of Ivan the Terrible".
The play, set in 16th century Moscow, depicts a world of cloak-and-dagger intrigue at the court of the dying tsar as the ambitious young Boris Godunov and other noblemen jostle for position.

Lebed, sacked as national security chief on Thursday for what Yeltsin called his lack of team spirit and his naked ambition for the top job, could hardly have chosen a more symbolic drama after his four turbulent months in the Kremlin.
"The situation in the country is exactly the same (as it was then)," Lebed told reporters in his booming bass voice after the performance.
Asked whether he had learned anything from the tale of Ivan's gloomy, chaotic last days of power, he said with a broad grin: "I've learned how not to run a country."

Wearing a dark suit, his wife on his arm, the 46-year-old former paratroop general oozed confidence, impishly addressing a scrum of journalists in the foyer with Godunov's rhetorical invocation "People of Moscow".

His vigorous manner contrasted with his former boss's haggard look in recent television appearances. Yeltsin, 65, is resting at a sanitorium outside Moscow ahead of heart surgery expected to take place next month.

Lebed has declined to criticise Yeltsin's decision to fire him, saying it would be impolite to speak ill of the sick but making clear he believed that Kremlin chief-of-staff Anatoly Chubais and other rivals engineered his dismissal.

Russian theatre-goers were not slow to draw a link between Yeltsin and Tsar Ivan, who in Tolstoy's play appears as a sick, half-deranged character haunted by premonitions of death and the memory of the son and heir whom he killed with his own hands.
"We always seem to end up with sick rulers. We need someone young and strong but also cunning," said one middle-aged woman.
She said Lebed, like the young Boris Godunov who later became tsar, was an outsider who took on the powerful political establishment.
"Lebed is not a diplomat. He speaks the truth. That's why they got rid of him," she said, adding that Lebed could still become Russia's next ruler.
Around 11 million Russians voted for Lebed in the first round of June's presidential elections in which he finished third. A recent opinion poll said he was the country's most trusted politician.
"We have a very complicated situation in Russia," said elderly theatre-goer Maria Petrovna. "But Lebed, like all Russians, is a fighter. He will battle on."
